source.title: In-Context Linear Regression Demystified: Training Dynamics and Mechanistic Interpretability of Multi-Head Softmax Attention
source.authors: Jianliang He; Xintian Pan; Siyu Chen; Zhuoran Yang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own superposition result in multi-task in-context regression, a different setting from the cited toy-model account. It measures task sharing across attention heads, not the feature-direction geometry or sparsity conditions specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The multi-task experiments report head/task allocation and explicitly describe superposition. Those results are recorded below. The paper’s citations to Toy Models of Superposition and other studies are not recorded as results from this study. It does not test sparse feature co-activation, nearly orthogonal feature directions, LLM feature structure, or SAE features.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the term 'superposition' from Toy Models of Superposition to describe one attention head serving two regression tasks with opposite-sign components (H=3, N=2). It never measures features stored as overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity, polysemantic neurons, LLM feature spread, SAE features or feature dimensionality. Task-to-head multiplexing in a one-layer softmax-attention regression model is a related but different construct (heads and tasks, not neurons and sparse features), so it tests no version. The record's 'tests/T3' is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. More precisely: H=1 and H=2 use shared weights across tasks, H≥2N gives dedicated head pairs, and 2<H<2N shows a run-dependent 'superposition' in which heads encode both tasks. The authors frame this as distributing capacity under constrained head count, and call a general characterization future work.
record.recipe_differences: The cited original is a toy-model study of feature superposition; this paper trains one-layer multi-head softmax attention on synthetic in-context linear regression and studies task-to-head allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported allocation changes with head count relative to task count. For H=3 and N=2, the paper says the learned pattern varies across repeated runs.

fits_no_version.finding: In two-task in-context linear regression (d=6, L=40, overlapping supports), H=1 and H=2 learn one shared weighted predictor, and H=4 assigns an exclusive head pair to each task. At H=3, one head acts as a negative head for Task 1 and a positive head for Task 2, and the aggregate still implements two independent debiased GD predictors. The H=3 pattern varied across runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When attention-head count is below what dedicated per-task allocation requires, trained attention can multiplex several tasks within single heads via sign-split components, recovering the per-task solution in aggregate.

record.problems: The multi-task experiment is a single small setup (N=2, d=6, L=40). The paper says the H=3 pattern varies across repeated runs but gives no quantitative run-level uncertainty or aggregate. Its task/head results do not establish sparse feature activation or geometric properties of feature directions.

untested.parts: All: no sparse features exceeding dimensions, no direction geometry, no sparsity transition.
All: no neurons or feature-importance allocation. The head/task capacity analogy is outside the version's construct.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's main contributions (KQ/OV patterns, debiased GD, length generalization, anisotropic covariates) are unrelated to superposition. The term is cited to Elhage et al. 2022 only as an analogy. Figure 19's table gives the H=3 per-head parameters, e.g. Head 3 μ̆ = -2.87 (Task 1) and 4.74 (Task 2); these could enrich r3 but bear on no version. There is a single small configuration and no run-level statistics.

versions.untested_parts: No test of sparse features exceeding representational dimensions, feature-direction geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric arrangements.
The study examines task allocation across attention heads, not polysemantic neurons or importance-based dedication of neuron dimensions.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure.
No LLM feature-distribution or sparse-feature recovery experiments.
No SAE dictionary-feature completeness, stability, or canonicality experiments.
No test of whether superposed features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: multi-head attention model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the learned task-to-head allocation in two-task linear regression.
rows.measure: Learned KQ feature weights and whether the head separates or shares task representations
rows.value: The single head learned one weighted kernel regressor for both tasks; the shared features {3, 4} received higher weights (∼0.5) than other diagonal entries (∼0.42).
rows.note: The paper reports a shared weighted predictor, not feature-direction geometry or a test of polysemantic neurons.

rows.subject: multi-head attention model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the learned task-to-head allocation in two-task linear regression.
rows.measure: Learned KQ and OV patterns and task prediction mechanism
rows.value: The heads learned opposing positive-negative patterns and a shared weighted pre-conditioned GD predictor; the overlapping features {3, 4} received slightly larger weights (∼0.13 vs. ∼0.12).
rows.note: The paper describes a shared predictor across tasks, not superposition of feature directions.

rows.subject: multi-head attention model
rows.operation_detail: Measured head contributions to each task and the resulting task-specific KQ patterns.
rows.measure: Whether heads encode and contribute to multiple tasks; task prediction mechanism
rows.value: All three heads contributed to both tasks. Head 3 had negative components for Task 1 and positive components for Task 2; the aggregate model was reported to implement the two independent debiased GD predictors through superposition.
rows.note: The paper says the observed pattern varied across repeated runs; the reported H=3 example is the described superposition case.
rows.check: State 'observed' has no version to be judged against. The row measures head sharing across two regression tasks, not feature or neuron superposition. The paper also says the H=3 pattern 'varies in repeated runs' and gives no run counts.

rows.subject: multi-head attention model
rows.operation_detail: Measured head allocation to tasks and task-specific feature supports.
rows.measure: Whether heads are shared across tasks or allocated to separate tasks
rows.value: Heads 1 and 2 were coupled to solve Task 1 using S1; Heads 3 and 4 were coupled to solve Task 2 using S2. The paper reports independent task-specific debiased GD predictors, with each head used exclusively for one task.
rows.note: This is the paper’s sufficient-head-capacity regime (H≥2N), not a test of the claim’s sparse-feature or direction-geometry conditions.
rows.check: State 'absent' has no version to be judged against. Dedicated head pairs per task at H=4 measure no claim version.
